Name: About CLPs
Description: A CLP (Cultural Life Program) is Furman University's program that encourages students to attend a variety of high-quality cultural, artistic, and intellectual events. Students are required to earn a set number of CLP credits to graduate, exposing them to diverse perspectives and enriching experiences outside the classroom.

Name: Law and Leadership Worldwide
Description:
Furman University's annual student program honoring the life and legacy of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr will be held on Thursday, January 15, 2026. This fireside chat guest is Justice Leona Theron, an eminent jurist and women's rights advocate from South Africa. The event is open to Furman alumni, students, faculty, staff, and friends of the University.

Sponsor(s): Franklin Ellis

Name: Kinoshita Kabuki Kanjincho
Description:
Kinoshita Kabuki Kanjincho Dress Rehearsal with a Q&A by the founder of Kinoshita Kabuki himself about this innovative reinterpretation of the famous Kabuki play, which depicts a tragic 12th-century hero, Yoshitsune, as Benkei, his loyal monk-samurai, who disguises their group as monks to pass the Ataka barrier. Based on the Noh play Ataka, it highlights loyalty, deception, and tense verbal sparring with the guard Togashi, and has become one of kabuki's most iconic, dynamic classics.

Sponsor(s): Shusuke Yagi

Name: Building the Beloved Community
Description:
Furman University's annual Community Breakfast honoring the life and legacy of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. will be held on Friday, January 16, 2026. This year's keynote speaker is Justice Leona Theron, an eminent jurist and women's rights advocate from South Africa. The event is open to Furman alumni, students, faculty, staff, and friends of the university.

Sponsor(s): Chandra Dillard

Name: Hearts of Glass CLP
Description:
Join the Furman Institutes for a compelling evening that brings together film, conversation, and community. The event will feature a special screening of Hearts of Glass, an award-winning documentary about entrepreneurship, sustainability, disability inclusion, health and well-being, and community impact. Following the screening, we will host a dynamic panel discussion with the Executive Directors of the Furman University Institutes, the film's director, and voices featured in the film. Together, we will consider how the stories and ideas in the documentary can inspire meaningful dialogue, action, and change. The event will serve as a platform to thoughtfully examine how the themes and issues presented in the documentary intersect with the specific needs, challenges, and aspirations of our local community. By fostering informed dialogue and encouraging the exchange of ideas, the discussion aims to inspire collaborative efforts, promote civic engagement, and identify actionable steps that can lead to meaningful, lasting improvements in the well-being and resilience of our community.

Sponsor(s): Loretta Crowley

Name: Measuring Fairness in Electoral Maps
Description:
In this session, Dr. Casey Hawthorne (Mathematics) and Dr. Glen Halva-Neubauer (Politics and International Affairs) will examine gerrymandering, bringing together mathematical tools and political analysis. The goal of this discussion is to explore methods for measuring and mitigating gerrymandering. The professors will begin with a brief history of key legislation and court cases that have regulated the practice. They will then examine different ways scholars have evaluated the fairness of various maps. Much of the discussion will center on the upcoming Supreme Court case, Louisiana v. Callais, which will determine the continued role of the Voting Rights Act in the future of gerrymandering. Following the presentation, students will participate in structured small-group discussions, offering an opportunity to reflect on the material, share diverse viewpoints, and connect the topic to their roles as civic participants.

Sponsor(s): David Fleming

Name: The Science of Balance: Work-Family
Description:
What is work-life balance and why does it matter for our well-being, our workplaces, and the science of human behavior? In this talk, Dr. Julie Wayne - an Industrial/Organizational psychologist, Professor, and David C. Darnell Presidential Chair in Principled Leadership at Wake Forest - will trace the evolution of work-family research, sharing how her own thinking has developed alongside the field and highlighting the evidence we know today. She will discuss a project in which she is developing a video-based intervention to help people better self-regulate and build healthier balance between work and life. Together, we'll explore the past, present, and future of this important area where psychological science informs everyday practice.

Sponsor(s): Grace Binion, Adam Putnam

Name: Jessica Lambert - artist talk
Description:
Jessica Lambert will discuss her current exhibition, Sportsball, on view at the Thompson Art Gallery. Her work explores competition, endurance, and sports through physically demanding performances and playfully constructed sculptures. By blurring the lines between athlete/artist, studio/gym, and exhibition/arena, she create a space for viewers to take on the role of spectators, fans, or athletes. The project is influenced by her experiences as a former D1 athlete and watching football, basketball, and volleyball. A reception of food and drink will precede the CLP, starting at 4:30pm. Students only need to attend the artist talk to earn CLP credit.

Sponsor(s): Stephen Mandravelis

Name: Church Music Conference "Big Sing"
Description:
The 2026 Furman University Church Music Conference and Residency will feature a celebration of Black Sacred Music with a special focus on the contributions of Andrae Crouch and his influence on gospel music and how his work impacted so many other musical genres. Guest Headliners and presenters for this conference include Dr. Stephen Newby and Dr. Robert Darden and their work leading to the release and tour of "Soon and Very Soon: The Transformative Music and Ministry of Andrae Crouch" (https://soonandverysoontour.com/) alongside musicologist and theorist Dr. Horace Maxile, composer Reginal Wright, vocalist Sylvia Jones, and Furman alumnus Tyrese Byrd '20.

Sponsor(s): Stephen Gusukuma

Name: The Story of Black History Month
Description:
Remembering, Reframing, and Reclaiming: The Story of Black History Month is a panel-style event designed to provide Furman students with insight into the development and significance of Black History Month. The panel will feature faculty and students, including Dr. Kaniqua Robinson, Dr. Holly Pinheiro, Tanu Madhavara, Laken Robinson, and Gabrielle Harvey. Through insightful responses from these panelists, attendees will gain a well-rounded understanding of the essence of Black History Month from multiple perspectives. This event is intended to kick off Black History Month activities at Furman University.

Sponsor(s): Kaniqua Robinson

Name: Uncivil Resistance and Queer Activism
Description:
This talk will discuss the kinds of resistance that the queer liberation movement has mobilized against the silencing and stigmatization of gender and sexual minorities. Professor Jose Medina of Northwestern University will argue that the fight against stigmatizing social exclusion requires the creation of a counter-community through uncivil protest actions. His talk will focus on multiracial queer activism and the social silences that differently racialized queer activists fight. Examples will include the Cooper Do-nuts Riot of 1959 in L.A., the Stonewall Riots of 1969 in New York City, and the visibility actions of Queer Nation in the 1990s.

Sponsor(s): Kathleen Casey

Name: Sustainable Crafting
Description:
Join Grant Cothran, the Founder and Executive Director of ReCraft Creative Reuse Center and Professor John Quinn to explore the intersection of sustainability and creative reuse. Dr. Quinn will share the pressing environmental concerns of escalating waste streams, resource constraints, and the environmental costs of linear production systems. Grant Cothran will follow by demonstrating that creative reuse centers illustrate cultural change, local action, and systems thinking. The session will conclude with an interactive "upcycling" activity, allowing participants to experience the creative reuse process firsthand using salvaged materials.

Sponsor(s): John Quinn

Name: Divine 9 Greek Showcase
Description:
The Divine Nine Greek Showcase is a dynamic Black History Month program that honors the history, service, and cultural impact of historically Black fraternities and sororities through education, storytelling, and performance. Hosted by Alpha Kappa Alpha Sorority, Inc. (Rho Zeta Chapter), Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. (Xi Omega Chapter), and Sigma Gamma Rho Sorority, Inc. (Eta Sigma Sigma Chapter), the showcase will feature presentations and strolling from Omega Psi Phi Fraternity, Inc., Zeta Phi Beta Sorority, Inc., Delta Sigma Theta Sorority, Inc., and Phi Beta Sigma Fraternity, Inc., followed by a moderated Q&A on the enduring role of the Divine Nine in campus and community life. The evening will include remarks from guest speaker Stephanie Rainey, Esq., and will be emceed by Dr. Ashley Johnson, celebrating tradition, accuracy, and unity across generations.

Sponsor(s): Kaniqua Robinson

Name: Varieties of Modern Paganism
Description:
"Interfaith Harmony: Varieties of Modern Paganism" is a lunch and learn in celebration of the United Nations' global Interfaith Harmony Week. This event will focus on modern pagan religions. Modern Paganism is a broad academic term encompassing a great many new religious movements, though most also draw from pre-Christian and sometimes indigenous traditions. What brought about the surge of interest in the mid-20th century in witchcraft, Druidry, heathenry, Goddess worship, and many eclectic forms of belief and practice? Holli S. Emore, MDiv is the Executive Director and a faculty member for Cherry Hill Seminary which provides graduate education for those serving Pagan and nature-based spiritualities. Emore is the author of Constellated Ministry: A Guide for Those Serving Today's Pagans (Equinox, 2021).

Sponsor(s): Alexis Carter Thomas

Name: Reconstructing Democracy
Description:
Professor Patricia Sullivan of the University of South Carolina History Department will expand the chronology of the Civil Rights Movement in a way that brings new goals and tactics into sharper focus. She will portray the movement as a "democracy" movement across several generations. The title and the central theme of the talk are inspired by W.E.B. Du Bois' book Black Reconstruction, published in 1935. In his book, Du Bois challenged prevailing interpretations that the struggle for Black rights during Reconstruction was a tragic mistake.

Sponsor(s): Stephen O'Neill

Name: AND IT WAS VERY GOOD
Description:
Dr. R. J. Snell will explore what it means for the book of Genesis to be more than just a descriptive account of the creation and first families of humanity, but how it is also prescriptive. It can be read as a call to embodying a particular moral vision and a narrative template for a life well lived. It is a story in which human beings are called to take an active part as image bearers. He will invite participants to explore questions of meaning and purpose like: What does it mean to be made in the image of God? What does it mean to be part of the story of Genesis? Dr. Snell will discuss personhood and how our understanding of personhood has evolved and continues to evolve - especially in light of the growing presence of AI. What does it mean to be human? To be conscious? To be a steward of creation? These are important questions for students to consider and have trustworthy resources for their critical reflection.

Sponsor(s): David Fink

Name: The Legal Fight Against Revenge Porn
Description:
A 2017 national survey by the Cyber Civil Rights Initiative of more than 3,000 adults found that 1 out of every 8 social media users has been a target of nonconsensual pornography, and the issue has become more widespread since 2017. Sharing intimate images or videos of someone without their consent is a serious violation of their privacy and dignity. It is an act of betrayal that can cause lasting emotional harm and can have societal implications far beyond the individual depicted in the images. Approximately 84% of people whose intimate photos and videos are shared without permission experience negative outcomes, including depression and PTSD, as well as social and academic impacts. Moreover, the threat of sharing explicit images is a tool that abusers use to trap partners in a relationship when they want to leave. This threat is also used to coerce victims into other exploitative situations, including into human trafficking. In 2025, South Carolina became final state in the nation to criminalize the nonconsensual distribution of intimate images.   Hear from a South Carolina state lawmaker who helped pass a law to prevent this form of abuse when South Carolina became the final state to pass a "revenge porn" law, as well as two attorneys who will discuss the societal and legal impacts of this crime and the ways this legislation will address those impacts.

Sponsor(s): Melissa Nichols

Name: The Sankofa Museum
Description:
The Sankofa Museum is a nationally touring educational exhibit that brings authentic American history directly to schools, colleges, libraries, and community organizations. Through rare artifacts, historical documents, photographs, and curated storytelling, the museum offers an immersive, evidence-based exploration of the Americana experience. The museum's name, Sankofa, reflects the idea of learning from the past to better understand the present. True to this purpose, the exhibit invites visitors to engage with more than a century and a half of American history through carefully preserved primary sources and interpretive guidance. The artifacts illuminate important periods of American history, including: (1) the eras of enslavement and emancipation, (2) the transformation of the nation during Reconstruction, (3) the rise of new leadership, innovation, and cultural contributions, and (4) major moments of social progress and national change. 

Sponsor(s): Holly Pinheiro, Jr., Rod Kelley

Name: Afrofuturism fireside chat
Description:
This fireside chat examines Afrofuturism as an interdisciplinary intellectual framework that engages history, culture, philosophy, and speculative thought. Afrofuturism offers a critical lens for understanding how Black communities have imagined alternative futures in response to historical exclusion from dominant narratives of progress, technology, and modernity. Through guided conversation, the speaker will situate Afrofuturism within broader scholarly discussions about time, memory, power, and social transformation.

Sponsor(s): Franklin Ellis

Name: Catching a Second Wind
Description:
The search for meaning and purpose can be quite elusive, and it can be even more challenging when the "meaning of meaning" is unclear.  There are many appropriate ways to approach the topic of calling, and an awareness of these various perspectives can be enlightening.  It is also the case that even when one discovers a sense of purpose for themselves, things can change --- and lead to a "back to the drawing board" experience that can be simultaneously discouraging and energizing.  This presentation will offer attendees the opportunity to learn of the approaches and to hear the story of someone who has experienced these shifts of purpose.  Dr. Tony McDade is the retired Executive Director of United Ministries in Greenville, an organization that focuses on housing stability, economic mobility, and homeless services.  Prior to that he was Executive Director of the Greenville Area Interfaith Hospitality Network.  Tony's journey is a helpful one to hear, not only for the expertise it demonstrates in important areas, but also for the experiences of pivoting when his calling seemed to change.

Sponsor(s): John Harris

Name: Furman: A Bicentennial History
Description:
In anticipation of Furman's 200 year anniversary, President Davis commissioned a bicentennial history of the university. Dr. Courtney Tollison and a team of two students (Emily Anne Harris '25 and Bryant Garrison '25), later joined by a third (Pender Raymond '27), researched and examined thousands of images. The authors will discuss the process of researching and writing an institutional history of a liberal arts college and will reveal the various processes behind it, from concept to its arrival on campus. 

Sponsor(s): Courtney Tollison

Name: Furman Lecture Series in Linguistics
Description:
In her talk, Dr. Tracey Weldon will explore the linguistic and cultural experiences of middle-class African Americans through an autoethnographic lens. Drawing on personal recordings across diverse settings, she will examine how speakers navigate the standard-vernacular continuum and highlight the underrepresented segment of the African American speech community. This talk underscores the need to broaden sociolinguistic definitions of African American English beyond working-class contexts.

Sponsor(s): Carole Salmon

Name: CSA Chinese Lunar New Year Celebration
Description:
Please join the Chinese Student Association and Dr. Eiho Baba to exlore the cultural, historical, and contemporary significance of the Chinese Lunar New Year. Come learn and have fun while experiencing traditional Chinese cultural activities and enjoying a selection of food options.

Dr. Eiho Baba is half-Chinese and half-Japanese. He holds a joint-appointment as an Associate Professor in the Department of Philosophy and the Department of Asian Studies at Furman University. Dr. Baba specializes in comparative philosophy, Chinese philosophy, Japanese philosophy, and metaphysics. His Ph.D. studies in University of Hawaii focused on Chinese philosophy in appreciation and realization.

Sponsor(s): Alex Akulli

Name: IACH Women In Healthcare Event
Description:
Siloed healthcare negatively impacts health and well-being, while collaborative, interdisciplinary models lead to better health outcomes, higher patient satisfaction and engagement, and fewer complications, delays in treatment, and emergency visits. Join a dynamic group of Furman alumnae for a panel discussion exploring how diverse health professions can work together to enhance community health and well-being. The panelists will share insights from their respective fields, highlighting the intersection of physical, mental, and preventive care across the lifespan and illustrating how they work collaboratively across disciplines to support individuals, families, and communities. The discussion will also examine the ways in which healthcare delivery settings influence health outcomes and demonstrate how multiple access points across the healthcare system play a vital role in prevention, treatment, and long-term wellness. Through real-world examples, attendees will gain a deeper understanding of how interdisciplinary approaches strengthen community health and why collaboration across professions and care settings is essential for building healthier, more resilient communities.

Sponsor(s): Loretta Crowley

Name: Gen-Z & the Future of American Politics
Description:
This Cultural Life Program will feature a moderated panel discussion examining the role of Gen-Z in contemporary American politics. As the first generation to come of age entirely in the digital era and amid heightened political polarization, Gen Z is reshaping political participation, leadership pathways, and civic engagement in distinctive ways. This program places Gen-Z political involvement within a broader intellectual and social context by exploring how young people engage with democratic institutions, advocacy, governance, and electoral politics.

The discussion will consider generational shifts in political behavior, barriers to participation, and the responsibilities of institutions, such as universities and government, in fostering informed and ethical civic engagement. By bringing together perspectives from both national electoral politics and student governance, the program offers students an opportunity to critically engage with questions about representation, leadership, and the future of democracy.

The event is designed as an educational discussion rather than a workshop, student organization activity, or political campaign event.

Sponsor(s): Kate Kaup

Name: You Decide: Is it Constitutional?
Description:
This  program situates the U.S. Supreme Court's work in the broader context of American constitutional democracy, where constitutional interpretation shapes rights, governance, and political conflict. 

As a structured academic exercise in constitutional reasoning, participants will practice close reading of constitutional text, including how scholars and judges argue from the document when it is silent or ambiguous on modern issues.

Sponsor(s): Maya Russell

Name: The Church and Global Peace
Description:
How has the Christian church (writ large) contributed to peace and prosperity in the past? Does it have a role to play in the contemporary world? Prominent Christian international relations and foreign policy scholar Mark Amstutz (Wheaton College) will address these questions in a lecture entitled, "Can the Church Contribute to Global Peace and Prosperity?" A response panel comprised of Professors Amstutz and Peter Feaver (Duke), plus retired American diplomat Larry Richter, will discuss the lecture and other issues surrounding the role of religion in foreign policy. The event will end with an audience Q&A.

Sponsor(s): Brent Nelsen

Name: THE IMPORTANCE OF BEING EARNEST
Description:
A comedy so sharp, it still stings.

Oscar Wilde's most celebrated play is a dazzling farce of mistaken identities, secret lives, and far too many cucumber sandwiches. Packed with biting wit, absurd romance, and some of the most quotable lines in theatre history, The Importance of Being Earnest remains a sparkling satire of appearances, ambition, and-above all-the art of not taking life too seriously. Link for tickets: https://furmantheatre.ludus.com/

Sponsor(s): Maegan Azar, Rhett Bryson

Name: American Military and the Culture Wars
Description:
Professor Peter Feaver (Duke University), an accomplished scholar and public intellectual focused on military-civilian relations, will speak on how the American culture wars are affecting the US military. His lecture will be followed by a panel discussion to include foreign policy expert Mark Amstutz (Wheaton College), retired diplomat Larry Richter, and Furman professor of military science LTC Paul Lew. An audience Q&A will conclude the event.

Sponsor(s): Brent Nelsen

Name: Gentrification in Black Communities
Description:
Dr. Jaime McCauley, scholar of social movements, social change, and environmental sociology, and Dr. Jen Mokos, interdisciplinary community geographer interested in relationships between knowledge production, culture, and the environment, will lead a talk exploring how flooding connects to long-standing struggles for justice in Bucksport, a historic Black, Gullah-Geechee community on the South Carolina coast. Bucksport has experienced repeated catastrophic floods that damage homes and strain resources, even as rapid growth and development pressures in Horry County threaten community land and culture. This talk highlights how residents and community partners have collaborated on community-engaged projects-from housing assessments and rain garden installations to advocacy and planning-to address these challenges and advocate for fair solutions. Hear how students have been involved in this work and learn how engaging communities for environmental justice can help protect people and places.

Sponsor(s): Franklin Ellis

Name: Emerging Artists
Description:
Join the Furman Symphony Orchestra, under the direction of Maestro Stephan Fillare, for an evening celebrating vibrant color, rhythmic energy, and expressive storytelling in orchestral music. The program features George Gershwin's Three Preludes, presented in an adaptation by Furman student Thomas Witt that brings Gershwin's unmistakable blend of jazz and classical style to the orchestral stage.

The concert also showcases the 2025-2026 Concerto Competition winners in two featured solo performances: Caroline James, flute, appears in Gordon Jacob's Concerto for Flute and Strings, a work prized for its lyricism and clarity, while Rebecca Wirth, saxophone, performs Jacques Ibert's Concertino da Camera, a virtuosic and colorful highlight of the saxophone repertoire.

Also featured is William Grant Still's Symphony No. 3, "The Sunday Symphony," an uplifting and reflective work inspired by the rhythms and spirit of African American church music, offering a radiant and affirming musical experience.

Sponsor(s): Stephan Fillare

 Adults: $20
Seniors 60+ / Furman Faculty & Staff: $15
Students: $10
Furman Students: $0 with I.D. - at the door

Name: COM Colloquium: Building our Classroom
Description:
Dr. Michelle Garland is serving as program planner for the Instructional Development Division of the International Communication Association for the upcoming 2026 conference. Based on her own research as well as her recent review of hundreds of scholarly works, Dr. Garland will use this colloquium to share current trends and issues in this vibrant research area and to explore the research methods prevalent in Instructional Communication Research. Her research explores the ways communication theory can inform the roles students and faculty play while co-creating meaningful classroom experiences. Also, this event occurs on Dr. Garland's birthday and this is her present to us!

Like this session, all Communication Colloquium events explore issues and ideas germane to the academic study of communication in its many forms. The communication studies department values many epistemologies and ways of researching societal questions. The series is intended to open this conversation to the wider campus and student audiences, bringing faculty research and student engagement into conversation.

Sponsor(s): John McArthur, Adam Richards

Name: Swiftynomics: Women and Our Economy
Description:
Join Furman University Libraries and the Department of Economics for a Book Talk with Dr. Misty L. Heggeness who will be discussing her new book Swiftynomics: How Women Mastermind and Redefine Our Economy. Dr. Heggeness uses the life and work of economic force and global icon Taylor Swift to examine the hidden contributions and aspirations of women-spotlighting the unmeasured value they create by pursuing their own ambitions. She challenges outdated narratives about women's roles in the economy, revealing the sheer volume of productive activity embedded in their daily lives-and the structural barriers that persist.

Sponsor(s): Elizabeth Sanford Middleton

Name: Liberal Arts Faculty Excellence
Description:
From the earliest educational and wisdom traditions, the fine arts-art, music, and drama, have played a central role in shaping what it means to be an educated person. From this perspective, they have also been foundational to liberal arts education, whose aims include the formation of judgment and civic character. This tradition continues globally, nationally, and here at Furman.

This program features a panel of Furman faculty and instructors from the Art, Music, and Theatre Arts departments reflect on their work as teachers, artist-scholars, and mentors, and on the role of the fine arts within the liberal arts tradition. The panel includes Sue Samuels and Matt Olson (Music); Kevin Kao and Stephen Mandravelis (Art); and Caroline Davis (Theatre Arts). Panelists will also consider the impact they hope their teaching, creative work, and engagement with students will have, both on students themselves and, by extension, on the world they inhabit.

Sponsor(s): Cynthia King

Name: Generational Advantage
Description:
Generations work alongside one another with various technologies - each with different communication norms, expectations, and definitions of trust. In this keynote, students will learn to critically examine stereotypes and myths about other generations, while also learning the research about techniques that work:  expectation management, strategic communication, and trust building across working styles and career stages.

Bowden's firm does original research on generational and workplace expectations. For example, four surveys administered during 2025 showed that 60.4% see communication etiquette as their top professional challenge. Boomers may want a phone call, GenX may want their emails answered, GenZ needs a text. Communication breaks down from vague expectations (79.1%), avoidance of tough conversations (65.6%), inconsistent follow up (54.6%) and lack of role clarity (39.6%). Boomers expect AI productivity enhancements, while Gen Z is skeptical of its ethical use. 78% of employers think they have solved AI adoption, while only 39% of their employees agree. Boomers feel outdated and feel rising ageism, while GenZ and Millennials lack mentorship. These kinds of insights combine workforce reports by independent firms, Gallup polls on generational difference, and GPS's surveys to examine the situation and offer researched solutions.

Sponsor(s): Brandon Inabinet

Name: Second Chances? Dialogue on Opportunity
Description:
Join in guided intergroup dialogue with your peers to consider what justice and opportunity really mean. After learning about the realities and barriers faced by people returning to their communities after prison, students will participate in purposefully guided intergroup table dialogue, skillfully moderated and facilitated by Riley Institute staff and Advance Team students, to unpack assumptions, examine challenges, and imagine how they can be part of meaningful social change.

Sponsor(s): Julie Meredith

Name: Artist Talk: ToastLab Opening Reception
Description:
Join True Inspiration Artist-in-Residence Alexa Wheeler for the opening reception for ToastLab, an evolving exhibition centered on women's stories as vital forms of shared knowledge, care, and memory. Through prints, video, textiles, books, and sculptural objects, Wheeler's interdisciplinary work reflects on everyday experiences-labor, inheritance, resilience, and transformation-that shape all of our lives, even when they remain unspoken. Installed as a living archive rather than a static display, ToastLab invites visitors to slow down, witness, and reflect, with the exhibition shaped over time through viewers' shared presence and participation. Wheeler will give a talk discussing her artistic practice, influences, and plans for the residency, as well as explain how ToastLab will continue to grow through collective engagement. A reception of food and drink will precede the talk, starting at 5:45 pm. Participation in the exhibition is not required for CLP credit.

Sponsor(s): Stephen Mandravelis

Name: Democracy's Future in the Age of AI
Description:
Jim VandeHei, co-founder of POLITICO and Axios and CEO of Axios, will explore how artificial intelligence is reshaping politics, journalism, and public trust. Drawing on his experience building major news organizations and covering national politics, VandeHei will offer a big-picture account of how information, technology, and political power interact in today's media environment and what those shifts may mean for the future of democracy. The event will include time for audience questions and discussion.

This CLP is co-sponsored by Furman's On Discourse initiative, which supports campus programming that encourages constructive engagement with diverse viewpoints on important public issues.

Sponsor(s): David Fleming

Name: "Memorable Melodies" Band Concert
Description:
"Memorable Melodies" is a special concert band performance offered by members of the Poinsett Wind Symphony and Furman University Bands.  Presented during the Region One Honor Band Clinic, the program features familiar tunes delivered in the concert band medium.  Jupiter from Gustav Holst's suite The Planets, a haunting arrangement of Shenandoah by Omar Thomas, folk songs from Percy Grainger's Lincolnshire Posy, and a rhapsody on Funiculi, Funicula are included in the program.  Dr. Buddy Deshler, Furman's professor of trumpet, is the featured soloist on Tico, Tico.  Music by Tara Islas and Henry Fillmore round out the program.  The free concert begins at 7:30 p.m. in McAlister Auditorium.  Please join us for a wonderful evening of "memorable melodies!

Sponsor(s): Sue Samuels, David Stanley

Name: AI's Influence on Marketing Culture
Description:
This CLP includes leaders and storytellers in Furman's creative community and invites attendees to critically examine the ways in which Generative AI is shaping our creative culture and communication strategies. A diverse group of specialists from the media, marketing, and public relations industry will provide their insight into one of our most significant cultural shifts in terms of creativity, communication, and human agency.

Panelists will share their diverse views on how Generative AI is impacting their artistic expression, identity as creators and communicators, and thoughts about this trajectory's impact on our creative culture. The questions posed by the moderator will challenge attendees to think critically about how AI-assisted tools are quickly reshaping the role of human agency in creative communication. For instance, is there still creativity in pivoting to prompt writing. In doing so, does our creative culture risk shifting from being primarily "creators" to "prompt curators" as we lean into automation and algorithms. From the panelists' expertise and moderated questions, this CLP aspires to have attendees reflect on where both the human intuition and professional creative judgement fit in a world of increasingly Generative AI-assisted creativity and communication.

Sponsor(s): John McArthur

Name: Advocacy Journeys That Shape Communities
Description:
How might expertise, professional experience, and sustained commitment be mobilized to advance the health and well-being of communities? This event brings together distinguished leaders in community health to explore how professionals across disciplines can use their voices to advocate for promoting population health and community well-being. Through a keynote address and moderated panel discussion, speakers will reflect on their respective advocacy journeys, illustrating how research, professional practice, and public policy can be strategically aligned to effect meaningful change. Drawing on scholarship, civic engagement, and clinical practice, panelists will discuss how purpose-driven advocacy translates disciplinary knowledge into tangible action and concrete initiatives that strengthen communities and advance public health outcomes. Participants will leave with an enhanced understanding of the mechanisms through which informed advocacy operates, as well as knowledge of evidence-based approaches to civic engagement and cross-sector collaborations that improve health outcomes and shape healthier, more resilient communities.

Sponsor(s): Loretta Crowley

Name: The Simril(l)s: Family in Black & White
Description:
Before dawn on May 5, 1871, paralyzed preacher Rev. Elias Hill lay in bed as the Ku Klux Klan rode toward his door. Hill could not stand, but he would not be silenced. With his niece Harriet Simril, Hill became a key witness in one of the first federal convictions of Klan terrorists-and then led 166 freedmen on an exodus from South Carolina to Liberia in search of freedom and rebirth.

For more than a century, their story remained hidden-even from their descendants and the descendants of their attackers. Today, two of those descendants-Spenser Simrill Jr. and Michael Simril-share their journey of reckoning, reunion, and remembrance with the CNN documentary Meet the Simril(l)s: A Family in Black and White as shown on The Whole Story with Anderson Cooper.

Sponsor(s): Margaret Oakes

Name: Haunted by God: The Life of Dorothy Day
Description:
A compelling one-woman show, HAUNTED BY GOD:  THE LIFE OF DOROTHY DAY, is a dramatic portrait of the co-founder of the Catholic Worker movement and one of the most outspoken and influential American Catholics of the 20th century. The production incorporates all the wit and prophetic grit of Day's own words about war, peace, American society, compassion, and protest in the spirit of Jesus. The New York Times eulogized Dorothy Day as a "nonviolent social radical of luminous personality." Produced in association with Call to Action.

Sponsor(s): Claude Stulting

Name: Beyond Bars: Pathways to Reentry
Description:
The United States leads the world in incarceration rates -driven by deep economic and racial inequities, and the impacts of one's criminal background continue even after their time served is finished. Limited access to jobs, housing, and financial resources creates a cycle in which incarceration and poverty reinforce one another, affecting families and broader communities. 

Join Jerry Blessingame, author, community leader, and Executive Director of Soteria Community Development Corporation, and Furman sociology professor Dr. Geniece Crawford Monde, for a panel discussion on breaking these cycles. Drawing on lived experiences, research, and community leadership, Blassingame and Monde will discuss the historical context behind current inequities fueling mass incarceration and barriers to opportunity after prison. After landscaping the issues, speakers will engage in a meaningful, solutions-oriented dialogue on policy solutions and practical pathways to reentry.

Sponsor(s): Julie Meredith

Name: Talk it. Do it. Dialogue and Debate
Description:
How we engage one another is as important as the topics we engage. It shapes whether our conversations are constructive, destructive, or lead nowhere at all. This program focuses on the differences among debate, dialogue, and deliberation as distinct forms of discourse. Brandon Inabinet, Professor of Communication Studies, and Andy Coe, Intergroup Dialogue Instructor, will provide an overview of the historical contexts and modern traditions from which these approaches emerged, as well as the research, goals, and guiding vision for their use in civil discourse and deliberation. The session will include small-group, roundtable conversations that invite participants to further explore and understand the differences between, and appropriate contexts for, these forms of engagement.

Sponsor(s): Cynthia King, Brandon Inabinet, Andy Coe

Name: Ramadan: Turning to God
Description:
Ramadan is the holiest month in Islam, observed by nearly two billion Muslims worldwide. During this month, Muslims fast from dawn to sunset, refraining from food and drink while dedicating themselves to prayer, reflection, charity, and spiritual renewal.

In this lecture, Dr. M. Taha Kasim will introduce the meaning and practice of Ramadan in Muslim life. The presentation will explore the historical origins of Ramadan, including its connection to the first revelation of the Quran in 610 CE, and explain the spiritual goals of fasting such as self-discipline, humility, compassion for those facing poverty, and renewed devotion to God.

The event will also place Ramadan in a broader comparative context, inviting students to reflect on fasting practices across religious traditions. A Q&A session will allow students to ask questions and engage in conversation about the religious, social, and ethical dimensions of Ramadan in contemporary Muslim communities.

Sponsor(s): M. Taha Kasim

Name: Democracy and Protest-Social Movements
Description:
Democracy thrives when citizens actively participate in shaping their society through ways beyond voting. Social movements, through protests, collective action, and public assembly, are fundamental to how democracy functions and evolves. In this session, Dr. Camille Lewis, Assistant Professor in the Department of Communication, will lead a discussion examining how social movements have transformed democracy in the Us by expanding participation, challenging injustice, and holding institutions accountable. The session will include small-group, roundtable conversations inviting participants to explore the vital relationship between civic engagement, dissent, and democratic life.

Sponsor(s): Cynthia King

Name: How We Love Love Songs
Description:
"How We Love Love Songs: Taylor Swift, Personal Attachments, and Beauty"

A CLP Talk by Dr. John Dyck

In this talk, Dr. John Dyck investigates the nature of love songs through the lens of analytic philosophy, providing students with both an illustration of how contemporary philosophy works, and a new and enriching way to look at something they engage with in at least a passive way nearly every day.

Dr. Dyck examines the common idea that aesthetic appreciation must be disinterested and objective, free from partiality or personal investment. At first glance, this view seems to exclude love songs from the realm of genuine aesthetic appreciation, since love songs are saturated with special interest and are often used "from the inside" to express subjective feelings toward a beloved. Dr. Dyck surveys existing responses to this tension: some reject the ideal of disinterested appreciation, while others conclude that love songs, however appealing, cannot qualify as objects of true aesthetic judgment. He argues, however, that we should retain the notion of disinterest-and that, properly understood, love songs can in fact meet its requirements.

Sponsor(s): Darren Hick

Name: Swimming In Data
Description:
Kate Douglass and Paige Madden, Team USA Olympic medalists at both Tokyo and Paris, and former students of mathematician Ken Ono at the University of Virginia, reunite with their mentor for Swimming in Data, a high-energy journey into the numbers behind gold medal performances. Douglass, a multiple world champion and world record holder, and Madden, a star of Team USA in distance freestyle, reveal what it feels like when every stroke, turn, and breath is captured and analyzed. Ono opens the black box, showing how mathematics, physics, and modern artificial intelligence transform video, sensor readings, and race splits into clear insights that change how athletes train and compete. Together, they share stories from practice pools and Olympic finals, inviting the audience to see elite sport in a brand new way, where great races are powered not only by talent and grit but also by beautiful ideas from mathematics.

Sponsor(s): Kevin Treu

Name: A Year of Impact: Dr. K Renee Horton
Description:
"A Year of Impact: Dr. K Renee Horton" is a thought-provoking lecture and discussion that explores the broad cultural, scientific, and social significance of Dr. K Renee Horton's contributions to STEM, diversity, and community engagement. Framed within the larger context of equity in science and the role of innovative leadership in shaping inclusive academic and professional cultures, this event highlights how Dr. Horton's work transcends technical achievements to address enduring questions about representation, access, and intellectual empowerment in the scientific world. Attendees will be invited to reflect on the intersections of science, society, and cultural change in the 21st century, gaining insight into how individual leadership can influence broader cultural understanding and community well-being.

The program will feature a presentation of Dr. Horton's work, including her professional accomplishments and impact on STEM inclusion, followed by a moderated Q&A session to encourage audience engagement. By situating Dr. Horton's story within larger academic and cultural conversations, this event will not only inform but also challenge students to consider how expertise, identity, and social context interact in contemporary scientific practice.

Sponsor(s): Courtney Kucera

Name: Furman Symphonic Band Concert
Description:
The Furman University Symphonic Band concert on March 13 is presented in conjunction with the South Carolina All-State Band, which brings hundreds of students from across the state to campus for three days of musical experience.  The diverse program features "Songs and Dances."  Percy Grainger's seminal folk song suite, Lincolnshire Posy, anchors the concert.  Dr. Mark Britt, professor of music, is the featured trombone soloist on Gareth Wood's Dance Sequence.  And, Dr. Cynthia Johnston Turner, who is the 2026 conductor of the Senior All-State Band, will appear as a guest conductor for Oscar Navarro's ecstatic Downey Overture.  More music by Nicole Piunno, David Gillingham, and Jacques Press round out the program.  Please join us for a memorable concert with wonderful music, Friday, March 13 at 7:30 p.m. in McAlister Auditorium.  The event is free and open to the public

Sponsor(s): Sue Samuels, David Stanley

Name: A Multilogue Between/Among Religions
Description:
Despite various longstanding and ongoing attempts at interreligious and intercultural dialogue and engagement as well as a surplus of good intentions, understanding across boundaries still seems to be remote. This lecture will examine the reasons for our difficulties to understand those who are conceived of as others, the methods used to facilitate interreligious understanding, and the power structures driving efforts in interreligious and intercultural engagement. Using the notion of "anekntavda" and the image of Indra's as well as the discursive strategies of Kitar Nishida, Risaku Mutai, Anthony Appiah, and Judith Butler, Gereon Kopf introduces the notion of the "multilogue." This discursive strategy, which differs from Franz Wimmer's "polylogue," re-envisions the way we think about "religious traditions" and "cultures," the boundaries that separate them, and the engagement between the members who claim and/or are assigned to particular religious and cultural identities. Finally, it introduces the little known 12-Wolf-Encounter Pictures in order to provide a metapsychology of identity politics and the establishment of hegemonies and to suggest a radical new way of interreligious and intercultural engagement that is neither top-down nor bottom-up but decentralized and inside-out

Sponsor(s): Alfons Teipen

Name: Reclaiming the Center
Description:
In this session, Dr. Kate Kaup (Politics and International Affairs/Asian Studies) and Dr. Brent Nelsen (Politics and International Affairs) will examine how people across the political left and right think about protecting democracy and advancing their interests in a time of polarization. The program will explore competing strategies for civic engagement and political action, while also asking where common ground may still exist across ideological difference. A central focus of the discussion will be how citizens with different commitments can still talk with one another, work together, and protect shared democratic interests. Following the presentation, students will participate in structured small-group discussions, offering an opportunity to reflect on the material, share diverse viewpoints, and connect the topic to their roles as civic participants.

This event is part of the On Discourse Initiative's Democracy Teaching Series, which provides programs designed to help students and the campus community deepen their understanding of democracy in the United States.

Sponsor(s): David Fleming

Name: America, Europe, and Globalization
Description:
Globalization is the process of interconnecting the peoples of the world through the movement of goods, services, capital, labor, and ideas across borders. Globalization accelerated in the years after the Berlin Wall fell, allowing Russia, Eastern Europe, and China to join the global economic system. The process, however, has slowed as anti-globalization political movements have gained influence, particularly in the United States under Donald Trump. Josef Braml will assess the current state of globalization from his perspective as a European and the director of the Trilateral Commission, Europe. His lecture will be followed by a panel discussion and audience Q&A.

Sponsor(s): Brent Nelsen

Name: Democracy and Justice
Description:
In this session Dr. Geniece Monde (Sociology) will moderate a conversation examining the intersection of democracy and the United States' criminal justice system. The goal of this discussion is for attendees to gain insight from practitioners and criminal justice scholars about how signature events, laws and policies shape present-day understanding of the criminal justice system. Most of the panel discussion with center on how democracy, or the ability of citizenry to decide how leaders and policies impact their lives, is made manifest through our complex systems that enforce laws, interpret legals and exact punishment. This will be a panel style discussion, featuring four experts in criminal justice: Mark Yancey of USC Law School, Dr. Kristen Lloyd, a criminal justice professor at Clemson, Rev. Hillary Taylor, the executive director of South Carolinians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty and Jerry Blassingame, the executive director of Soteria. Dr. Monde will ask panelists questions about their understanding of the criminal justice system based on their expertise and experience and how they approach criminal justice through a democracy informed lens. After the discussion, members of the audience will have an opportunity to ask questions from the panelists.

Sponsor(s): Geniece Crawford Monde

Name: Freedom Seekers and Their Stories
Description:
Prior to the publication of COMBEE (winner of the 2025 Pulitzer Prize in History), historians of slavery had slave narratives and WPA interviews to tell the history of enslaved people in their own words and from their own perspectives. COMBEE uses the US Civil War Pension Files and slave holders' documents to identify the enslaved people who escaped enslavement on seven rice plantations on the Combahee River Raid, tracing them backwards into enslavement and forward into freedom. This lecture will introduce the enslaved people liberated in the Combahee River Raid and the sources Fields-Black used to identify these freedom seekers, tell their stories, and document the largest slave revolt in US history.

Sponsor(s): Courtney Tollison

Name: FUISA's International Dance Festival
Description:
The FUISA International Dance Festival is an annual event that brings traditional dances,music, rhythms, and attire from around the world to Furman's mainstage. Come explore, enjoy, and learn about the significance of traditional dances from around the world represented by international students at Furman University. At this event participants will have the opportunity to engage and learn about global cultures and celebrate the mosaic of global diversity at Furman University.

Sponsor(s): Alex Akulli

Name: Medieval Interlingual translations
Description:
Dr. Olivier Bertrand, a specialist in French medieval linguistics, explores how translations into French during the Middle Ages reveal a richly complex and fragmented linguistic landscape. Spanning more than seven centuries-from the Strasbourg Oaths to the great translation projects of the fifteenth century-his talk highlights the coexistence of multiple languages, regional dialects, and social and stylistic registers across medieval France. Drawing on manuscript evidence, Dr. Bertrand shows how translation offers a unique lens for understanding the evolution and diversity of medieval French during a formative period in its history.

Sponsor(s): Carole Salmon

Name: Global Perspectives in Liberal Arts
Description:
The event "Experiencing Internationality: How Global Perspectives Enrich Teaching and Learning in Liberal Arts Education" will engage international faculty and students to share their lived experiences and academic journeys, highlighting the vital role internationality plays in shaping inquiry, pedagogy, and campus life. Through reflective discussion, participants will explore how diverse cultural perspectives deepen classroom dialogue, challenge assumptions, and foster more inclusive approaches to teaching and learning within the liberal arts. The conversation underscores internationality as a dynamic force that strengthens intellectual curiosity, mutual understanding, and academic excellence.

Sponsor(s): Cynthia King

Name: Globalization. Discuss.
Description:
This On Discourse event will explore the costs and benefits of globalization. Scott Lincicome of the Cato Institute and Mark DiPlacido of American Compass will present their differing perspectives on globalization in brief presentations. Moderator Brent Nelsen (Furman) will then invite participants to work through a series of questions at their tables, encouraging them to articulate their positions while listening to those who might disagree. Trained student facilitators placed at each of the round tables will ensure discussions remain civil and constructive.  

For those unfamiliar with the issue, globalization is the process of interconnecting the peoples of the world through the movement of goods, services, capital, labor, and ideas across borders. Some support globalization as a positive development in the post-Cold War world. It has lowered costs, increased consumer choice, and lifted as many as a billion people out of poverty. Others see the process as harmful to people vulnerable to the loss of jobs to lower-cost workers, environmental degradation and climate change, and the elimination of local culture.

Sponsor(s): Brent Nelsen

Name: Living Like a Friar
Description:
Furman Alumnus Father Casey Cole will give a lecture/talk about his life as a Franciscan Friar. The traditions of Mendicant orders of Friars date back to the 13th century with a focus on vows of poverty and service to local communities. Fr. Cole will present on how emulating these traits of Catholic Friars can improve one's enjoyment of life.

Sponsor(s): Brian Goess

Name: Professional Leadership in the Age of AI
Description:
This program, led by Duke Law professor Jeff Ward, examines how leaders of tomorrow must understand how to approach emerging technologies. Already artificial intelligence (AI) tools are reshaping the flow of news and information, predicting the creditworthiness of our consumers, allocating finite resources and benefits, influencing the sentencing of our convicted, and carrying people across roads, rails, and skies with increasingly limited human involvement. This is the dawn of the Age of AI.

Are we ready for an AI-fueled future? Probably not. Surely our legal, ethical, cultural, and professional frameworks must evolve. This CLP aims to help each of us, the future legal professionals, the future health professionals, the changemaking innovators and entrepreneurs, and the policymakers of tomorrow become active participants in and leaders of this evolution.

Sponsor(s): Maya Russell

Name: COM Colloquium: Ethical World Making
Description:
Based on her paper presented at the National Communication Association Conference in November 2025, Dr. Mai Nou Xiong-Gum will explore the tension between disparate approaches to refuge, refugees, and home. The paper emphasizes the epistemic and material precarity of displacement shaped by war, climate catastrophe, and structural violence rooted in colonial, racial, and capitalist histories. Her work examines the embodied negotiation of refugee identity, media portrayals, gendered oppression, and intergenerational trauma and theorizes refuge as a dynamic, relational process of power, identity, and belonging within global and intercultural frameworks.

Sponsor(s): John McArthur

Name: Transformative International Education
Description:
How has international education contributed to peace and prosperity in the past? Does it have a role in the changing geopolitics and future of globalism? Join us for an engaging conversation with Dr. Karoly Jokay,  Executive Director of the Hungarian-American Fulbright Commission, as we explore diverse perspectives on international education as a force that fosters peace, prosperity, and stability at home and abroad. The event will conclude with Q&A from the audience.

Sponsor(s): Alex Akulli

Name: Health & Well-Being of Young Adults
Description:
Please join the Institute for the Advancement of Community Health, the Earle Student Health Center, and Student Life for a collaborative discussion examining the challenges and opportunities to support young adults' health and well-being during the transition to adult care. Across the United States, health outcomes for young adults are often compromised, as this population frequently faces difficulties navigating the healthcare system and may lack the knowledge needed to independently manage their own health care needs. According to an article published in the Journal of Pediatrics in October 2025, "only 18% of youth, with and without special health care needs, received health care transition preparation services from their health care professionals."

Sponsor(s): Loretta Crowley

Name: Teach. Talk. Do. Listening to Understand
Description:
In this program, Dr. Zachary White will lead an interactive lecture and discussion on empathetic listening and the power of storytelling. Through conversation and small-group activities, participants will use My Neighbor's Voice listening cards to explore how hearing others' stories fosters understanding and connection, civic responsibility, and cultural awareness. Each table will have a facilitator to provide instructions, with trained dialogue facilitators supporting the experience throughout. This program emphasizes the power of listening and reflection on what it truly means to hear one another.

Sponsor(s): Cynthia King, David Fleming

Name: Toastlab Closing Reflection
Description:
Join us for the closing reception of Toastlab, the Spring '26 Artist-in-Residence exhibition by Alexa Wheeler. This interdisciplinary, participatory exhibition explores often-unspoken stories of labor, inheritance, resilience, and transformation in women's lives, and how those experiences circulate collectively. This culminating event invites students, faculty, and community members to reflect on the exhibition's evolution through shared participation and its role as a living archive. The program will include remarks by Wheeler on how the exhibition's initial goals shifted as ideas developed through individual contributions; reflections from exhibition participants who wish to share their experiences; and a short scholarly and personal response by Dr. Sarah Archino, Chair of the Department of Art, reflecting on the project as a collective endeavor. The evening will also offer a final opportunity for attendees to contribute voices, experiences, or reflections before the exhibition concludes. A light reception of food and drink will precede the program, beginning at 4:30 pm. Participation in the exhibition is not required for CLP credit.

Sponsor(s): Stephen Mandravelis

Name: Opioid Safety: Substance Use and STIs
Description:
This presentation will focus on opioid safety and the intersection of substance use and sexually transmitted infections (STIs). A panel of experts will present on STIs, HIV, and opioid drug use and provide contextual information as it relates to South Carolina. Presented by the South Carolina Department of Public Health, and Furman University Responders. 

Sponsor(s): TJ Banisaukas

Name: Film: Herzog's "Theatre of Thought"
Description:
"Theatre of Thought" is a captivating exploration of the human mind through the lens of legendary filmmaker Werner Herzog. In this film, Herzog delves into the complexities of consciousness, the mysteries of the human mind, and the nature of thought itself, engaging with leading experts from various fields. With his signature blend of philosophical inquiry and cinematic artistry, Herzog invites audiences to question the very essence of what it means to be human. A mesmerizing journey into the depths of the mind, "Theater of Thought" challenges perceptions and sparks introspection about our inner worlds. After the screening, Dr. Freeman (Neuroscience) and Dr. Simmons (Philosophy) will host a short discussion of the big ideas presented in the documentary.

Sponsor(s): Aaron Simmons, Linnea Freeman

Name: Sex in the Dark
Description:
Sex in the Dark is an annual event where students can anonymously ask our panel of experts questions about sexuality, gender, relationships, and identity in an open, intellectual space. The event aims to educate and foster meaningful conversations about complex social and cultural issues surrounding different kinds of relationships and identities, offering a safe and inclusive environment for exploration. Lights will be dimmed while the Q&A panel answers questions aimed at broadening your perspective of sexuality and relationships.

Sponsor(s): Gwen Hirko

Name: Women's Power in the Revolution
Description:
The American Revolution was a war for independence. Yet during this conflict, ordinary American women claimed their dependence on husbands, on officials from local institutions, and on the state itself-all patriarchal forces that governed their lives. In this presentation, Dr. Jacqueline Beatty, Associate Professor of History at York College of Pennsylvania and author of In Dependence: Women and the Patriarchal State in Revolutionary America, will explore the experiences of women who submitted thousands of petitions in the Revolutionary era, demanding remuneration, clemency, property rights, and even divorces, all using language that parroted presumptions of their legal, economic, and social subordination to men. Yet this rhetoric belied the purposeful strategies women employed in their petitions to patriarchal officials. Ultimately, women in the revolutionary era were able to advocate for themselves and express a relative degree of power not in spite of their dependent status, but because of it.

Sponsor(s): Kathleen Casey

Name: Dance Spectacular
Description:
Join Furman Dance for "Dance Spectacular," an end-of-year showcase in McAlister Auditorium! The Furman Dance Team showcases its performances throughout the season, featuring solos, duets, and trios. Various styles of dance will take center stage such as hip hop, contemporary, pom, jazz, and tap. This performance is free of charge and open to the public.

Sponsor(s): Sue Samuels, David Stanley, Tiffany DuPuy

Name: Palm & Passion Service
Description:
Palm and Passion, a service of songs and lessons, will take place on Palm Sunday--March 29, 2026. This event marks the beginning of Holy Week in the Christian tradition. Palm and Passion is a celebration and remembrance of the life of Christ during the week leading up to his crucifixion. There have been a variety of ways to commemorate this occasion that expanded with the Protestant Reformation of the sixteenth century. During the service at Daniel Chapel, Palm and Passion will include readings by our members of our campus community and songs by the Furman Chamber Choir. The event will not only be a religious event, but it will be an educational experience grounded in the historical and contemporary significances of a widely celebrate tradition. All are welcome.

Sponsor(s): Alexis Carter Thomas

Name: A keynote lecture by Kaelynn Partlow
Description:
The Disability Rights Club will host a keynote lecture by Kaelynn Partlow, author of Life on the Bridge and featured participant on Netflix's Love on the Spectrum. In this lecture, Partlow will explore the intersection of her lived experience as an autistic individual and her professional work as a therapist, examining broader questions of neurodiversity, inclusion, and systemic understanding of autism. The event will situate disability rights within larger intellectual and social conversations, offering students the opportunity to engage critically with issues of identity, equity, and clinical practice. The lecture will include a moderated question-and-answer session to encourage thoughtful dialogue and student participation.

Sponsor(s): Loretta Crowley

Name: Inside SC Govt with Sen. Vincent Sheheen
Description:
Former South Carolina state senator Vincent Sheheen offers a clear, engaging look at how South Carolina's state government works - and why it matters - in his recently published book, A Concise Guide to South Carolina State Government. Drawing on his firsthand experience in the State House and stories of influential South Carolina political leaders, Sheheen breaks down the history, structure, and decision-making processes that shape life in the Palmetto State. This event is designed for students and community members who want to better understand state government and become more informed, engaged citizens.

Sponsor(s): Julie Meredith

Name: The Path to Community Health
Description:
Health and well-being are shaped by more than individual choices. National data on social determinants of health from Healthy People 2023 highlight that factors such as economic stability, education, and access to supportive services are key predictors of health outcomes. This moderated panel discussion will bring together leaders from across Greenville who work at key access points within the community. Panelists will share insights from their professional experiences in early childhood systems, language access in healthcare, health literacy, economic mobility, and community-based clinical care. Together, they will examine how an individual life experiences connect to broader patterns to helps students understand how the topics are not isolated issues but reflect systemic forces that shape community well-being. Through real-world examples rooted in Greenville, students will gain a deeper understanding of how social and economic conditions intersect with healthcare access. The discussion will also highlight practical solutions and collaborative strategies that are helping to clear pathways toward healthier, more equitable communities.

Sponsor(s): Loretta Crowley

Name: Exploring Native American Justice
Description:
Eastern Band Cherokee Tribal Court Associate Judge Sunshine Parker will join Furman Professors Danielle Vinson and Helen Lee Turner for a conversation on Native American Justice. The discussion will examine justice for Native Americans and tribes at several levels-between tribes and federal/state governments and within the tribes. Through the conversation, we will examine how Native American conceptions of horizontal justice compare to the typical vertical justice of the American judicial system and explore the challenges tribes and indigenous people face in gaining justice.

Sponsor(s): Danielle Vinson

Name: The Evolution of Gender in Labor Markets
Description:
Dr. Claudia Olivetti, the George J. Records 1956 Professor of Economics at Dartmouth College, will present a lecture on the evolution of gender in labor markets. Dr. Olivetti is a Research Associate at the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) and a co-director of NBER's Gender in the Economy Working Group. She was previously a professor of economics at Boston College and a fellow at the Harvard Radcliffe Institute. Her research focuses on women in the labor market, including wages, careers, and labor supply, as well as the historical and institutional forces shaping gender gaps in economic outcomes. Her work has appeared in leading economics journals including the American Economic Review, the Quarterly Journal of Economics, and the Journal of Political Economy.

Despite decades of progress expanding women's opportunities in the workplace, significant gender gaps in employment and earnings remain. This talk traces how economic research has evolved to understand these gaps, highlighting the distinction between differences in preferences and skills and the role of constraints and institutions. Drawing on decades of evidence, the lecture explores what drives persistent inequality and what it means for economic efficiency and policy.

Sponsor(s): M. Taha Kasim

Name: The Unitary American Executive. Discuss.
Description:
The American Constitution does not delineate the powers of the president in great detail. Presidents over the 250 years of American history have abided by a set of norms established as far back as the Washington Administration. Donald Trump has broken many of those norms in a move to expand presidential power using a relatively new legal doctrine known as the unitary executive. The theory is controversial, and its current application is far-reaching. The Tocqueville Center's year-long celebration of American independence continues with this On Discourse event that will feature Phillip Munoz (Notre Dame). Each scholar will outline his position. Students will then engage each other through a set of questions designed to help them think through the implications of different visions of presidential power. They will be encouraged to engage one another across their different opinions. The moderator will help them practice the skills (listening, empathy, etc.) necessary for civil discussion.

Sponsor(s): Brent Nelsen

Name: Heritage Spanish
Description:
Language judgments about what counts as "correct" or "appropriate" speech circulate widely in U.S. society and are closely tied to histories of race, migration, and power. Universities frequently articulate commitments to diversity and inclusion, yet they also function as institutional sites where these broader societal language ideologies are reproduced. Focusing on South Carolina - often described as part of the "New South" - this talk draws on recent data on language attitudes in higher education, as well as on classroom-based work with heritage learners of Spanish, to examine how such judgments shape students' sense of belonging, confidence, and legitimacy in college spaces. The talk explores common beliefs about Spanish, including assumptions about "pure" forms of the language, and shows how they circulate in university classrooms even when institutions aim to be inclusive. It also highlights how heritage-language classrooms can function as counter-spaces that challenge deficit views and recognize heritage students as skilled bilingual language users.

Sponsor(s): Stephanie Knouse

Name: Gilbert Allen Poetry Reading
Description:
Furman Professor of English Emeritus Gilbert Allen will read from his new book of poetry, Stanzas in America, to kick off campus events for National Poetry Month. Allen is the author of eight books of poetry and three collections of short stories. Stanzas in America is a witty and wry commentary on life in the United States in the second Tump administration. Combining elements of pop culture, internet memes, Shakespearean allusions, and reflections on the long scope of history, Allen's poems comment and challenge us as citizens to observe, react, and be more fully engaged with our cultural and civic life.

Sponsor(s): Jeffrey Makala

Name: A Dance With A Chance
Description:
The Furman Dance Club presents "A Dance with Chance," a performance celebrating Merce Cunningham, the twentieth-century American modern dance choreographer who pioneered chance-based approaches to artmaking.

Sponsor(s): Helen Joy

Name: Prayer: Stories & Practices
Description:
Prayer: Stories & Practice is a panel and roundtable that will explore various ideas of prayer as a cultural and religious concept and through the lenses of a variety of practices. Panelists, all Furman community members, will share from their training as religious professionals and practitioners, personal experiences, how their faith/tradition formed them to think about prayer. Additionally, they will discuss how they currently view and practice prayer as a religious and cultural activity. Following the panel discussion, there will be a Q & A session, and a time for participants to engage in roundtable discourse about their prayer stories and practices.

Sponsor(s): Alexis Carter Thomas, Vaughn CroweTipton

Name: Data Feminism in Action
Description:
As data and AI are increasingly mobilized in the service of global corporations, governments, and elite institutions, their unequal conditions of production, their inequitable impacts, and their asymmetrical silences become increasingly more apparent. It is precisely this power that makes it worth asking: "Data science by whom? AI for whom? In whose interest? Informed by whose values?" And most importantly, "How do we begin to imagine alternatives for data's collection, analysis, and communication?" In this talk, Dr. Ignazio will present "data feminism" principles, along with work from her most recent book, Counting Feminicide (MIT Press 2024). Drawing from a large-scale participatory action research project, she will describe how data activists enact alternative epistemological approaches to data science that center care, memory and justice. These informatic practices constitute a form of "epistemic disobedience" to the reigning logics of AI and data science. This talk, and the book that it draws from, make the case that grassroots data activists, predominantly from Latin America, are at the forefront of a data ethics that rigorously and consistently takes power and people into account.

Sponsor(s): Kathleen Casey

Name: STEM Scholarship in Liberal Arts
Description:
This panel discussion brings together STEM faculty from multiple STEM departments to highlight the role of scholarship and research in their field within liberal arts institutions. We will feature Dr. George Shields ( Drug Design and Computational Chemist), Dr. Gustavo Coelho ( Earth, Environmental, and Sustainability Sciences;  Water Resources Engineer ), Dr. Christian Millichap ( Mathematics; Scholar in Geometric Topology ), Dr. David Moffett ( Physics, Astronomer), Dr. Anna Cass ( Health Sciences, Epidemiologist), Dr. Min-Ken Liao ( Biology, Microbiologist), and Dr. Chris Alvin ( Computer Science Pedagogy and Best practices, Researcher of AI implementation in education). This program brings STEM faculty from multiple departments together for a conversation about their experiences as scientists and educators in a liberal arts setting. The conversation will explore teaching, mentorship, engaged learning, and research-driven curiosity, highlighting how a liberal arts environment fosters critical thinking and innovation in STEM.

Our panelists actively mentor undergraduate students in research projects as part of their scholarship agenda. Panelists will share insights into their research programs, discuss the integration of undergraduate students into scientific inquiry, and reflect on how the liberal arts environment fosters interdisciplinary thinking and innovation in STEM fields. We will learn how our panelists carry out scholarship in their fields of study while balancing the needs and commitments associated with a Liberal Arts education model.

Sponsor(s): Cynthia King

Name: HOLA/Film Club Film Showing CLP
Description:
HOLA and the Film Club are sponsoring a screening of the 2006 film "Quinceanera." Dr. Lozano-Alonso will introduce the film from a cultural perspective contextualizing the tradition of quinceaneras in the Mexican American community as well as social issues that are relevant to the community and presented in the film (such as gender roles, religion, social expectations, etc).

Sponsor(s): Angelica Lozano-Alonso

Name: The Painter's Fire: A Forgotten History
Description:
In honor of the 250th anniversary of the America's revolution, Zara Anishanslin, Associate Professor of History and Art History at the University of Delaware, will be discussing her new book The Painter's Fire: A Forgotten History of the Artists Who Championed the American Revolution.

This talk addresses the role that artists played in advancing the cause of liberty in the American Revolution. Anishanslin illustrates that the war was not only fought in the colonies by soldiers with muskets and bayonets, but that on both sides of the Atlantic, artists also played an integral role in forging revolutionary ideals. She will discuss the intertwined lives of three largely forgotten Patriot artists: Robert Edge Pine, Prince Demah, and Patience Wright who not only defied the British monarchy but also worked as spies. Armed with paint, canvas, wax, they risked their lives and reputations to support the cause of American liberty.

Sponsor(s): Carolyn Day

Name: Furman Symphonic Band Concert
Description:
The Furman University Symphonic Band is pleased to present an outdoor "pops" concert on Saturday, April 11 at 2:00 p.m.  Bring your chairs and picnic to Furman's Amphitheater and share in familiar tunes that will leave you clapping, dancing, and singing along.  The event is free and open to the public.

Name: FU Percussion Ensemble Spring Concert
Description:
The internationally-acclaimed Furman University Percussion Ensemble will perform its Spring 2026 Concert featuring guest composer/performer Ian Chang, as well as members of the percussion ensemble from Greenville's Fine Arts Center.

The Furman Percussion Ensemble is proud to host Academy Award and BAFTA-nominated musician, composer, and producer Ian Chang in their first in-person collaborative performance. Known for his impressive roster of progressive pop collaborators such as Moses Sumney, Joan As Policewoman, and Matthew Dear, Ian also performs and records as a member of Landlady and the experimental trio Son Lux with whom he scored A24's Best Picture winner Everything Everywhere All at Once as well as Marvel Studios' 2025 film Thunderbolts*.

Admission: Furman students FREE with I.D. $5 suggested donation at the door
