Name: Bending the Arc: Screening & Discussion
Description:
Join Furman Master of Science in Community Engaged Medicine (MS-CEM) students and the Institute for the Advancement of Community Health for a screening of the documentary Bending the Arc. The film tells the story of Paul Farmer, Jim Yong Kim, and Ophelia Dahl as they build Partners In Health, a nonprofit global health organization founded in 1987 that works to provide high-quality healthcare to the world's most vulnerable populations. The film screening will be followed by a panel discussion about the challenges of global health equity.

Sponsor(s): Loretta Crowley

Name: Who's in charge? Ethical Implications
Description:
Gerald C. (Jerry) Kane, a 1994 Furman graduate and religion major, returns to campus to explore one of the most pressing questions of our time: as artificial intelligence grows more powerful, what does it mean for our humanity? Now the C. Herman and Mary Virginia Terry Chair in Business Administration and Department Head of Management Information Systems at the University of Georgia's Terry College of Business, Kane brings a unique perspective that bridges the moral and philosophical questions at the heart of the liberal arts with the technological forces reshaping business and society.

The session will address critical questions across several dimensions of AI's societal impact: How do biases embedded in training data perpetuate and amplify existing inequalities? Why does the "black box" nature of AI decision-making pose fundamental challenges to transparency and accountability? What does widespread automation mean for the future of work and economic opportunity? How does the infrastructure powering AI contribute to growing environmental concerns? As AI systems enable unprecedented levels of data collection and behavioral monitoring, what does the erosion of privacy mean for individual freedom? How should educators and students rethink learning and academic integrity when AI can generate answers on demand? And perhaps most fundamentally, as AI systems increasingly make decisions on our behalf, are we at risk of ceding our autonomy - shifting from a world where humans use technology as a tool to one where technology begins to "use" us?

Sponsor(s): Helen Lee Turner

Name: A Reading with Poet Glenis Redmond
Description:
Glenis Redmond, Inaugural Poet Laureate Greenville and 2025 recipient of the Order of the Palmetto, will explore the culture and history of Greenville, the state of South Carolina, and beyond. Her work engages the lives of important figures like Dave "the Potter" Drake and Clayton "Peg Leg" Bates as well as the raced history of our state parks while celebrating what those parks offer to contemporary visitors. Students will find her dynamic passion compelling as they learn new details about their region and poetry.

Sponsor(s): James Engelhardt

Name: The Power of Connection:Community Health
Description:
Join the Institute for the Advance of Community Health for a keynote address by Risa Wilkerson, Executive Director of Healthy Places by Design, a nonprofit consulting group serving philanthropy, nonprofit, and community-based organizations across the United States. Risa Wilkerson is also the lead author of Socially Connected Communities: Solutions to Social Isolation and a contributor to the Stanford Social Innovation Review through her article A Sense of Belonging. This event will allow students the opportunity to learn from a nationally recognized expert in the fields of community health and design. By sharing research and real-world examples of successful initiatives lead by the Healthy Places By Design team, the keynote will address how loneliness and social isolation have quietly become public health challenges across the lifespan, impacting everything from physical wellness and mental health to academic performance, economic security, and civic participation and highlight interconnected factors that shape healthier, safer, and more resilient communities.

Name: COM Colloquium: TV at the Fringes
Description:
Based on her paper presented at the Society for Cinema and Media Studies Annual Conference in April 2026, Dr. Selena Dickey will explore the economic and political factors related to television infrastructure, access, and content distribution. The paper is titled "Television at the Fringes: Distribution, Geography, and History." This analysis explores the ways that structural factors beyond viewer control shape the types of media citizens are able to receive, creating vast disparities in media content and format.

Like this session, all Communication Colloquium events explore issues and ideas germane to the academic study of communication in its many forms. The communication studies department values many epistemologies and ways of researching societal questions. The series is intended to open this conversation to the wider campus and student audiences, bringing faculty research and student engagement into conversation.

Sponsor(s): John McArthur

Name: Competing Visions of Democracy
Description:
In this session, Dr. Kate Kaup will examine competing visions of democracy from around the world. The program will ask what makes a democracy a democracy and why different societies answer that question differently. Dr. Kaup will compare representative, representational, and deliberative approaches to democracy, asking whether democracy should be judged primarily by electoral procedures, by how well government reflects the public's interests, or by the quality of public reasoning and discussion. She will also highlight institutional differences across democratic systems, including parliamentary and presidential models. As part of the event, students will participate in structured small-group discussions, offering an opportunity to reflect on the material, share diverse viewpoints, and connect the topic to their roles as civic participants.

This event is part of the On Discourse initiative's Democracy Teaching Series, which provides programs designed to help students and the campus community deepen their understanding of democracy in the United States. The series addresses documented gaps in civic knowledge and is grounded in academic inquiry and open dialogue.

Sponsor(s): David Fleming

Name: False Starts: Meet the Author
Description:
Since Head Start began in the 1960s, policymakers and academics have celebrated preschool as an anti-poverty policy. Drawing on two years of observations that centered on children's experiences in two different preschools, Dr. Stockstill shows how preschools entrench rather than disrupt inequality. In no small part, this happens because preschools across the nation are more segregated than elementary, middle, or high schools. Dr. Stockstill reveals how such segregation plays out in the lives of children of color in one preschool and white, affluent children in another. Racism and the harshness of US poverty had troubling implications for children's time use, peer interaction, access to objects, and sense of closeness with teachers. Rather than give children a complete, early advantage, segregated preschools give children a false start to experiencing full membership in the social world of schools.

Sponsor(s): Joseph Merry

Name: Tens Across the Board
Description:
Racism and homophobia in the 1970s had a profound impact on Black and Latinx queer people. For those who were ostracized or disowned by their families, many sought refuge in large population centers like New York City. Areas like Harlem were known for their vibrant underground LGBTQIA+ subculture that offered orphaned queer folx a safe space for community. These efforts led to the creation of ballroom culture, known for its competitive expression through dance and fashion and the opportunity to join chosen families called "houses". Recent media generated awareness of ballroom culture through television series like "Pose" (2018) and reality TV competition shows like "Legendary" (2020). 

This event showcases the historical significance of ballroom for various communities of people and ballroom's influence on the present-day experiences of those actively involved in ballroom competition. A panel of three current members of a house will share their exposure to ballroom and speak to the influence ballroom has had on their personal development. This panel will also provide insight into the expansiveness of ballroom culture and the accessibility of those wishing to join. Panelists will reflect on popular culture's perceptions of the ballroom experience, addressing examples of language that originated within queer communities and how said vernacular entered the mainstream zeitgeist. Participants will learn how houses function within ballroom, the relevance of roles and titles within house, and the engagement of houses within competitive spaces. Panelists will demonstrate the intricacies of a ballroom competition, including the competitive categories in which participants compete and how participants are judged on their "look".

Sponsor(s): Judith Williams

Name: Street Scene, an American opera
Description:
The Sarah Reese Lyric Theatre at Furman University presents Street Scene, an English-language opera by Kurt Weill. Set over the course of two sweltering summer days on a New York City tenement stoop, the opera portrays the lives, struggles, and aspirations of immigrant working-class families living side by side in an urban community.

Often described as a "Broadway opera," Street Scene uniquely blends operatic technique with jazz, blues, and American popular song, creating a vivid and distinctly American musical language. The work is based on Elmer Rice's Pulitzer Prize-winning 1929 play of the same name, with lyrics by Langston Hughes. Together, these artists crafted a powerful portrait of American life-one that captures both the tensions and hopes of a diverse community and remains deeply relevant today.

Sponsor(s): Grant Knox

Name: Spring 2026 Drag Show
Description:
Join the Furman Pride Alliance for the Spring 2026 Furman Drag Show! Currently a topic of social and political debates, drag entertainment stretches from Burlesque (circa 1900) to the hit television show, "RuPaul's Drag Race" (2009-present). As an important part of U.S. cultural history, drag reflects evolving norms regarding gender expression, sexuality, and cross-dressing. After introductory remarks by Furman professor Dr. Scott Henderson about the history and contemporary controversies surrounding drag shows, several professional and student drag artists will perform. Time permitting, the drag artists and/or Dr. Henderson will answer questions after the performances.

Sponsor(s): Scott Henderson

Performers will include the Greenville Jazz Collective, Poinsett Winds, USAF Heritage Of America Band's Heritage Winds, The Foreign Landers, and more.
